cues.text: Luke , by strong and ancient tradition a native of Antioch in Syria, appears to have been a Gentile convert to the faith — the only writer of the New Testament not born a Jew — and a physician by profession, a detail St.
Paul himself confirms, addressing him in one epistle as "Luke the beloved physician."

Unlike the Apostles, Luke was almost certainly not an eyewitness to the events of Christ's earthly ministry; he tells us so himself in the careful opening lines of his Gospel, explaining that he has undertaken to compile an orderly account only after diligently investigating everything from eyewitness testimony passed down to him — the meticulous method of a trained mind accustomed to careful observation.

Luke first enters the narrative of Acts at Troas, where the account itself shifts abruptly into the first person plural — "we sought to go on into Macedonia" — a subtle but unmistakable sign that the author had personally joined Paul's missionary band at that very point.

From Troas onward, Luke's presence recurs throughout Acts wherever this same "we" reappears: crossing into Europe, journeying to Jerusalem, and remaining with Paul through the long, dangerous sea voyage and shipwreck that carried the Apostle finally to Rome — a companion who did not merely record Paul's missionary journeys from a distance but walked, sailed, and suffered through a considerable portion of them himself.

Luke's own Gospel reflects, more than any other, a particular tenderness toward those the ancient world was most inclined to overlook: it alone preserves the Nativity narrative largely as it must have come from Mary's own remembered testimony, the parables of the Prodigal Son and the Good Samaritan, and a sustained attention to women, to the poor, to tax collectors and sinners, and to the marginalized that has led the whole Christian tradition to call it, above the other three, the Gospel of Mercy .

A later, cherished tradition — impossible now to verify but treasured nonetheless — holds that Luke was also a painter, and that he made the very first portrait of the Blessed Virgin Mary; whether or not the tradition is literally true, it captures something genuine about a Gospel whose written portrait of Mary and of Christ's own mercy remains, in its own way, among the most vivid ever composed.
A Second Book for the Church

Luke did not stop with the story of Christ's earthly life; his second volume, the Acts of the Apostles , continues the narrative into the life of the young Church, tracing the Gospel's spread from Jerusalem to Rome itself and preserving, in the process, our only sustained historical account of the Apostolic age — a debt the whole Church owes to one careful physician's determination that this unfolding story, too, deserved to be set down accurately for those who would come after.
Luke's faithfulness to Paul did not waver even as the Apostle's own life drew toward its close.

In his final letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his execution, Paul laments that several companions have deserted him or been sent elsewhere, adding with evident and simple gratitude: "only Luke is with me."
Of all the friends and fellow workers who had accompanied Paul across decades of missionary labor, it was the quiet physician of Antioch who remained at his side until the very end.

Tradition holds that Luke, unmarried and remarkably long-lived for the ancient world, died in Greece — variously placed in Boeotia or Achaia — around the age of eighty-four, having outlived nearly all his companions from the great missionary age he had done so much to record.

Patron of physicians, surgeons, and artists, and represented in Christian art by the winged ox, a symbol drawn from his Gospel's opening scene in the Temple, Luke remains a model of the careful, humble scholarship that the Church has always needed alongside its more dramatic witnesses — proof that a physician's patient attention to evidence and a friend's quiet, unwavering loyalty can, together, leave behind two of the most treasured books the New Testament possesses.
